recipe-planner.name: Recipe planner
recipe-planner.description: Find recipes by ingredient, plan the week's meals, and build a shopping list.
recipe-planner.prompt: A recipe and meal planning app. Screens: Discover, with a search bar, ingredient filters, and recipe cards with photo, cooking time, and calories; Recipe, with ingredients, step-by-step instructions, and a button to add it to the plan; Meal plan, a weekly calendar with breakfast, lunch, and dinner slots; and Shopping list, which collects the ingredients from the plan, grouped by aisle, with checkboxes. Fresh, warm design with rounded cards and a green accent.

workout-tracker.name: Workout tracker
workout-tracker.description: Log workouts, time your sets, and watch your strength go up week by week.
workout-tracker.prompt: A workout tracking app. Screens: Today, showing the planned workout, a streak counter, and a start button; Workout, to log sets, reps, and weight for each exercise with a rest timer between sets; History, a list of past workouts by date with total volume; and Progress, with charts of personal records and weekly volume per muscle group. Bold, energetic design with a dark background and a bright orange accent.

budget-tracker.name: Budget tracker
budget-tracker.description: Track spending by category, set monthly budgets, and spot where money goes.
budget-tracker.prompt: A personal budget app. Screens: Overview, with this month's balance, spending against budget, and recent transactions; Add expense, a quick form with amount, category icons, date, and a note; Budgets, a monthly limit for each category with a progress bar that turns red when it's close; and Insights, with a spending-by-category donut chart and a month-by-month comparison. Calm, trustworthy design with a navy and teal palette.

salon-booking.name: Salon booking
salon-booking.description: Let clients browse services, pick a stylist, and book a time slot.
salon-booking.prompt: A booking app for a hair salon. Screens: Services, a list of services with price and duration grouped by category; Stylists, with photos, specialties, and ratings; Book, where the client picks a service, a stylist, a date, and an open time slot, then confirms; and My bookings, with upcoming and past appointments and options to reschedule or cancel. Elegant, modern design with a soft rose and charcoal palette.

local-events.name: Local events
local-events.description: Discover events nearby, RSVP, and see who else is going.
local-events.prompt: A local events and meetups app. Screens: Explore, with event cards showing a cover image, date, place, and category chips to filter by; Event, with details, a map location, the host, attendees' avatars, and an RSVP button; My events, a list of events I'm going to and ones I've hosted; and Profile, with my interests, past events, and a short bio. Vibrant, playful design with a purple and yellow palette.

team-tasks.name: Team tasks
team-tasks.description: Organize projects into boards, assign tasks, and track what's due.
team-tasks.prompt: A task manager for small teams. Screens: Projects, a list of projects with progress bars and member avatars; Board, a project's tasks in To do, In progress, and Done columns; Task, with title, description, assignee, due date, priority, and a checklist; and My tasks, everything assigned to me, sorted by due date with overdue tasks highlighted. Clean, minimal design with plenty of white space and a blue accent.

language-flashcards.name: Language flashcards
language-flashcards.description: Learn new words with flashcards, daily goals, and quick quizzes.
language-flashcards.prompt: A language learning flashcards app. Screens: Home, with today's goal, a streak, and decks to pick from; Study, a flashcard that flips to show the translation and an example sentence, with buttons for 'Again' and 'Got it'; Quiz, multiple-choice questions with a score at the end; and Word list, every word in a deck with search and a mastered badge. Friendly, encouraging design with bright colors and large, readable type.

pet-care.name: Pet care
pet-care.description: Keep every pet's meals, vet visits, and reminders in one place.
pet-care.prompt: A pet care app. Screens: My pets, cards for each pet with photo, name, and the next reminder; Pet profile, with breed, age, weight, and feeding notes; Reminders, for meals, walks, medication, and vet visits, with times and repeat options; and Health log, a timeline of vet visits, vaccinations, and weight. faq.subtitle: Can't find your answer? The <docs>docs</docs> cover every feature step by step.

builds.question: What does AppxPrompt build?
builds.answer: A real mobile app, written in Expo and React Native, that runs on iOS and Android and on the web. You describe it, the agent plans the screens with you, and then builds them one at a time while you watch.

coding.question: Do I need to know how to code?
coding.answer: No. You talk to the agent in plain language, and you can click any element in a screen to change its text, color, or image. If you do code, every file is there to read, and you can download the project.

ownership.question: Who owns the code?
ownership.answer: You do. Download a complete Expo project as a ZIP, or push it to your own GitHub repository, and keep working on it anywhere. Nothing ties it to AppxPrompt.

phone.question: How do I try my app on a phone?
phone.answer: Click {scanQr} in the workspace and scan it with Expo Go. The app opens on your phone, and every change you make shows up there right away while the tab stays open.

backend.question: Can my app have real accounts and data?
backend.answer: Yes. {connectBackend} gives your app its own CloudHike database, sign-in, and file storage, with no changes to your screens. Until then, apps run on sample data stored in your browser.

stores.question: Can I put my app in the App Store and Google Play?
stores.answer: On {proName}, {publish} builds the .aab, .apk, and .ipa files through your own Expo account, ready to upload with your Apple and Google developer accounts. Any plan can publish the app as a website with its own address.

screens.question: How many screens can an app have?
screens.answer: Up to {free} on {freeName} and {pro} on {proName}. The agent keeps a first plan small so you can see results quickly, and adds more screens whenever you ask.

cost.question: What does it cost?
cost.answer: Starting is free, with {signup, plural, one {# credit} other {# credits}} that never expire. A new screen costs {screen, plural, one {# credit} other {# credits}} and a round of changes costs {edit}, while chatting, planning, and switching themes are free. See <pricing>Pricing</pricing> for {proName}.

privacy.question: Who can see my projects?
privacy.answer: Only you, unless you choose otherwise. You can share a project with someone by email so they can view it, or show it on the AppxPrompt home page for anyone to try with sample data.

docs.heading: AppxPrompt docs
docs.subtitle: Everything you need to go from an idea to an app on your phone, and from there to the app stores.

getting-started.title: Getting started
getting-started.p1: AppxPrompt turns a description into a working Expo (React Native) app for iOS and Android. The whole journey takes a few minutes:
getting-started.step1: Describe your app in the box on the home page, or start from a <templates>template</templates>.
getting-started.step2: Answer a few questions from the agent, then confirm the screen plan it proposes.
getting-started.step3: Watch the screens being built, and tap through the running app in the preview.
getting-started.step4: Change anything by chatting, or click an element to edit it directly.
getting-started.step5: Try it on your phone, download the code, or publish it.
getting-started.p2: You need a free account to create a project. If you write a prompt first, it's kept while you sign up, and your project starts as soon as you're in.

writing-prompts.title: Write a good prompt
writing-prompts.p1: The agent asks about anything you leave out, but a clear prompt gets you to a good first version faster. Mention:
writing-prompts.item1: What the app is for and who uses it: "A booking app for a hair salon's clients."
writing-prompts.item2: The main screens and what each one shows: "a list of services with prices, and a calendar to pick a time."
writing-prompts.item3: The look you want: "elegant, soft rose and charcoal, rounded cards."
writing-prompts.p2: You can attach up to {count, plural, one {# file} other {# files}} to a prompt: screenshots of apps you like, sketches, a logo, or a PDF or text file with your requirements. Pick the platform from the menu next to {attach}.
writing-prompts.tip: Start small. A focused app with three or four screens is quicker to get right, and you can add more screens any time.

planning.title: Plan with the agent
planning.p1: When your workspace opens, the agent reads your prompt and asks a few short questions about what matters most. Questions often come with numbered choices, so you can answer with just a number, or type your own answer.
planning.p2: Then it proposes a plan: the screens it will build, what each does, and the tabs the app will have. Ask for changes in the chat ("add a settings screen", "drop the map") until it's right, then confirm with the button on the plan or by saying so. Nothing is built, and no credits are used, until you confirm.
planning.tip: Unless you ask for more, a first plan has a few main screens plus a sign-in screen, so you see results quickly.

building.title: How a build works
building.p1: Once you confirm, the agent builds your app in this order:
building.step1: Themes and data. The colors, fonts, and sample content your screens share.
building.step2: Shared components. Buttons, cards, and other pieces reused across screens, so one change updates the whole app.
building.step3: Screens, one at a time, each appearing in the preview as soon as it's ready.
building.p2: Builds run in the background, so you can leave the page and come back to follow along. Credits are taken when a build starts, and if it fails you get back the credits for whatever it didn't finish.

editing.title: Edit your app
editing.p1: Ask for any change in the chat: new screens, a different layout, extra fields, renamed tabs. Only the screens and components affected are rebuilt, and each one keeps working until its new version is ready.
editing.p2: Click the Edit icon on a screen in the canvas, then click any element to change its text, colors, or image. Edits show up instantly, without reloading the app, and are saved straight into the code. A selected element is also sent with your next chat message, so you can say "make this bigger" and the agent knows what you mean.
editing.p3: In edit mode, select an image to replace it with a link, generate a new one from a description, or transform it ("make it a watercolor"). Each AI image costs {credits}.
editing.tip: Colors you pick by hand stay the same when you switch themes. To keep an element in step with the theme, ask the agent instead.

themes.title: Themes
themes.p1: Every app comes with five themes: {default}, {ocean}, {forest}, {sunset}, and {midnight}, which is dark. Switch between them from the theme switcher in the workspace. Nothing is rebuilt and it's free, so try them all. Want something else? Ask the agent for a new theme in your brand colors.

phone.title: Test on your phone
phone.step3: Scan it with your iPhone's Camera, or from inside Expo Go on Android.
phone.p1: The app runs on your phone and updates live as you make changes. Keep the browser tab open while you test, because closing it takes the app offline.
phone.tip: Your app needs Expo Go for SDK 54. If Expo Go says the app is incompatible, it's on a newer SDK.

backend.title: Add a backend
backend.p1: New apps run on sample data stored in your browser, which is perfect for trying ideas. When you're ready for real users, click {button} in the workspace header and sign in to CloudHike.
backend.p2: Your app gets its own CloudHike project with a database, plus sign-in and file storage if its screens use them. Every collection in your app becomes a real table, and your screens don't need to change. Later builds keep the backend up to date on their own.

export.title: Export your code
export.p1: The code is yours. Open the {button} menu in the workspace header:
export.item1: {download} gives you a complete Expo project. Run npm install and npx expo start, then scan the QR code with Expo Go. The included README has the details.
export.item2: {push} connects your GitHub account and pushes to a repository you choose. The first push to an empty repository goes to its default branch. Every other push goes to a new appxprompt/… branch, so nothing already on GitHub is overwritten.

publish.title: Publish your app
publish.p1: Click {button} in the workspace header. Publishing runs through your own Expo account, so the first time you'll paste an Expo access token. AppxPrompt stores it encrypted and only uses it to publish your app and follow its progress.
publish.p2: {web} puts your app online at its own expo.app address. The address stays the same when you publish updates, and if an update fails the previous version stays online. Available on every plan.
publish.p3: On {pro}, Expo builds the files for you:
publish.item2: <file>.apk</file> to install directly on Android phones.
publish.item3: <file>.ipa</file> to upload to the App Store.
publish.p4: Android signing is set up for you. iOS builds need your Apple developer credentials in Expo, and the dialog walks you through it if they're missing. Keep the dialog open to follow a build's progress.

sharing.title: Share and showcase
sharing.p1: Projects are private by default. Choose {share} from the {export} menu to give someone with an AppxPrompt account view-only access by email. It shows up under "{shared}" on their home page.
sharing.p2: In the same dialog, turn on {showcase} to let anyone try your app. Visitors only ever see sample data, never your backend, and anything they do stays in their own browser.
sharing.p3: To try a variation without touching the original, duplicate a project from its menu on the home page.

credits.title: Plans and credits
credits.p1: A new screen costs {screenCredits}, a round of changes costs {edit, number, integer}, and an AI image costs {image, number, integer}. Chatting, planning, and switching themes are free, though the agent needs at least {editCredits} to reply. Your balance is always in the header. See <pricing>Pricing</pricing> for details.

used.question: When are credits used?
used.answer: When a build starts. A new screen costs {screenCredits} and a round of changes costs {edit, number, integer}, and a new screen added in that round costs {screen, number, integer} on top. If a build fails, you get back the credits for what it didn't finish.

rollover.question: Do my credits roll over?
rollover.answer: Free credits never expire. Pro's monthly credits expire at each renewal and are replaced with a new {monthly, number, integer}. Free credits you still have when you join Pro stay yours, and are used after the monthly ones.

downgrade.question: Can I downgrade at any time?
downgrade.answer: Yes. You keep Pro until the end of the period you've paid for, and then move to Free. Your projects stay yours, even if you have more than {max, number, integer}, but you can't start new ones beyond that.

publish.question: Can I publish on the Free plan?
publish.answer: Yes, as a website with its own address. Building .aab, .apk, and .ipa files for the app stores is part of Pro.
